newsitem.title: USA: Three killed in chemical plant explosion, fire.
newsitem.headline: Three killed in chemical plant explosion, fire.

text.p: Three firefighters were killed and 16 people were injured in an explosion and fire that ripped through a chemical plant near the Mississippi River on Thursday, spewing poisonous chemicals into the air.

The blast at the BPS Inc. chemical plant in West Helena, Arkansas, released a black plume of highly toxic chemicals used in insecticides and forced the evacuation of scores of residents in the path of the toxic cloud, officials said.
"It's bad. I don't know how much worse it's going to get. I'm not sure anybody knows right now," Arkansas State Police spokesman Wayne Jordan said, adding that the number of casualties could rise.

The early afternoon explosion flattened a large section of the plant and rocked the manufacturing and farming communities of Helena and West Helena located along the Mississippi River near the tri-state border with Tennessee and Mississippi.
It released azinphos-methyl, an insecticide that attacks the central nervous system and is used as a pesticide to control mites and other bugs, hazardous materials experts said.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry, traveling with President Bill Clinton in Costa Rica, said Clinton was "very concerned" about the explosion. "He knows the facility itself," McCurry said.
He said Clinton aide Bruce Lindsey, also from Arkansas, was getting more information on it for the president.
It was not clear whether the three firefighters were killed by flames or the chemicals.

Officials evacuated a nearby hospital and nursing home. Forty-four patients of the Phillips Regional Medical Center were moved out with some taken to another hospital and others to a local community college for housing overnight.
Authorities said smoke billowed across the river into Mississippi and the industrial park where the plant was located was still inaccessible on Thursday evening.
"We understand the fire is now under control, but officials there are asking people to remain out of the area," Arkansas Office of Emergency Services spokeswoman Francis Huddleston said.
Residents of both Helena and West Helena, which have a combined population of about 18,000, were told to stay indoors and keep shut their windows and doors.

Brief exposures to azinphos-methyl can generate symptoms ranging from breathing problems to paralysis. Longer exposures could cause permanent, degenerative damage to the central nervous system, University of Houston chemist James Cox said.
"If I were exposed to it I would regard it as exceedingly hazardous," Cox said.

Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee and his state health director Sandra Nichols flew to the area late Thurday to inspect the damage and state officials said they sent in large quantities of atrophine, a widely used antidote for the inhalation of toxic gases.
"They indicated to us they might need a substantial amount, and our people at the Office of Emergency Services took it from there," Huckabee's spokesman Grant Tennille said.
About half of the BPS Inc. plant was reduced to molten or twisted metal by the explosion and blaze.
A U.S. Coast Guard spokesman said shipping was halted along a 20-mile (32 km) section of the Mississippi River south of Memphis in response to the accident.
